Blisko Polski: 1939, Bloody Monday in Częstochowa
wPolsce24: On 4 September 1939 the Germans began a slaughter

content.p: On Monday 4 September 1939, the fourth day of the Second World War, German soldiers who had entered the Polish city of Częstochowa the day before began seizing civilians from the streets and from their homes and shooting them. The killing began after a burst of confused gunfire in the city that morning. Poland's Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) calls what followed one of the largest German war crimes against Polish civilians in September 1939. Polish history knows it as Bloody Monday.

Nobody has established exactly how many people died. A German battalion commander reported 99 shot. The city's authorities at the time estimated 671 dead. Bodies later recovered from graves number 227 in 1940 and 240 once the 2019 finds are added, and the IPN has also given an estimate of about 500. Historians stress that many victims were never found.
content.h2: A city taken without a fight
content.p: Częstochowa lay close to the German-Polish border, and before the war a large share of its women and children had been evacuated deeper into Poland. The 1939 census gave the city about 138,000 residents. The Polish 7th Infantry Division left on 2 September, and thousands of residents, many of them young men able to bear arms, left with the army, according to the history site Blisko Polski. German forces reached the city on 3 September and, by the accounts in that article, entered without a shot being fired by the population.

The IPN names the occupying force as the German 46th Infantry Division, commanded by Major General Paul von Hase. Blisko Polski says the 42nd Infantry Regiment of that division was sent in, and that German planners feared communist resistance in a working-class town. Around midday the German command settled in the town hall. The patrol reports written after the entry, the same article says, described a population that offered no resistance and obeyed orders.
content.h2: The shooting on the morning of 4 September
content.p: The trouble began in the late morning of 4 September, when shots were heard from two parts of the city. Blisko Polski places the first outbreak in the courtyard of the Trade and Industrial School, where soldiers were quartered. It places the second on Strażacka Street, where German troops were escorting a marching column of 300 to 400 Polish civilians who had been seized the day before. Witnesses disagreed about how long the shooting lasted: some said an hour, others a few minutes.

The same article says that, according to the documents available, the firing was set off by the inexperience and panic of young German soldiers, who afterwards said they had fired at imagined Polish partisans. It quotes two German accounts of the scene. A senior medical officer of the IV Army Corps recorded that tracer rounds striking house walls gave the impression of fire coming from windows. An officer wrote that almost everyone seemed to be shooting at everyone. A report by an Einsatzgruppe, a German unit, concluded that even if German troops had been attacked by civilians, by the end it was impossible to tell who was firing at whom.

The IPN says the cause of the incident has never been explained unambiguously. It gives the German losses as nine soldiers dead, among them two officers, and 14 wounded. Blisko Polski says eight soldiers died and 14 were wounded. The broadcaster wPolsce24, summarising the IPN, gives eight dead including two officers and 43 wounded, four of whom later died. These figures do not match, and none of the pages explains why.

The German command, by the account in Blisko Polski, blamed the civilian population. Blisko Polski also says that civilians in the marching column were hit in the confusion, and that witnesses afterwards spoke of as many as 200 dead there, a figure the article says appears greatly exaggerated in the documents that survive.

In revenge, according to the IPN, Wehrmacht soldiers began mass arrests of random people (the IPN's text puts the word in quotation marks). They stopped residents on the street or dragged them out of flats and the gateways of tenement houses. Those held included refugees from towns around Częstochowa as well as local people. Columns of hostages were marched to the central squares, to the empty barracks of the Polish army, to school grounds and to the city's cathedral. The IPN says about 10,000 people were collected on what was then Pieracki Square, now Biegański Square, alone; wPolsce24, summarising it, says this was by 5 p.m.

Executions began in many places at once. The IPN says soldiers shot men, women and even children on very petty pretexts, using single shots to the back of the head, machine-gun bursts, grenades and bayonets. The main killing grounds were Biegański Square and Daszyński Square, the square in front of the cathedral and the streets of the Old Town. Deep anti-aircraft trenches dug before the invasion were in many cases used as mass graves.

Blisko Polski adds detail from its own reading of the record. People in the squares were forced to stand for hours with their hands raised or to lie face down, and anyone who moved was shot in the back of the head. Men were separated from women and children and searched, and anyone found with so much as a razor or a penknife was killed, it says. It also reports that Jews were made to jump over an anti-aircraft trench and shot where they fell if they failed, and that people were killed in a military hospital marked with Red Cross emblems. These are that article's descriptions, and it names no source for them.

The Einsatzgruppe report mentioned above recorded that on 4 September its men shot two partisans caught in the act, one sniper and two Jewish assassins. Blisko Polski, which cites the report, says the Germans knew very well that no such partisan or resistance formations yet existed in Poland.

When the roundup was done, some children and women were released because there were too many prisoners. Blisko Polski says the men were sent to the cells of the prison at Zawodzie and to St Sigismund's church, and when those filled, into the cathedral. The IPN says that civilians were reportedly held as hostages in the cathedral on the night of 4 to 5 September, and that some of them did not return home. It adds that archival documents and aerial photographs supplied by a local historical association showed Polish anti-aircraft trenches in front of the cathedral.

Blisko Polski says soldiers kept bursting in to terrorise the prisoners with shots into the air and blind fire that killed some, and that those held there were forced to relieve themselves inside the church during two days of captivity. To guard against any revolt, the article says, the Germans then took 80 hostages, most of them Jewish members of the city's elite, and held them for several weeks in the barracks at Zawady.
The figures come from different kinds of evidence, and they do not add up to one answer.

ul.li: The German account. The commander of the 1st Battalion of the 42nd Infantry Regiment reported that 96 men and three women had been shot, according to Blisko Polski.
The city's count. The IPN and wPolsce24 say the Polish municipal authorities of the time estimated 671 people murdered and hundreds more wounded.

The 1940 exhumations. They were carried out with German consent. Blisko Polski says they were ordered by a German officer, Richard Wendler. They recovered 227 bodies from various burial sites, 194 men, 25 women and eight children, 205 of them Poles and 22 Jews. Only 121 of the 227 were identified. Blisko Polski stresses that this is not the full toll: killings at other sites, such as the barracks occupied by the Wehrmacht, are not included, and many families took their dead away themselves.

The 2019 finds. In July 2019, during renovation of John Paul II Square in front of the cathedral, workers came upon human remains. The IPN exhumed 13 people. Their possessions included boots, belts, buckles, a comb, a wallet with Polish pre-war coins, a pocket watch in a leather case and a copper wedding ring. The IPN and wPolsce24 add this to the 1940 figure to give 240 victims, 22 of them Polish citizens of Jewish origin.

Later estimates. A 2020 IPN notice says soldiers shot about 500 people, adults and children, and another IPN item that year says it is estimated that about 500 died. Blisko Polski gives a range of 227 to as many as 500 Polish and Jewish residents.

content.p: The IPN adds that the remains of many victims have never been found and that many places where graves are thought to lie have never been excavated.

The violence did not end in one day. Blisko Polski says that on 5 September soldiers shot seven members of two families near the airfield, and that notices ordered residents to hand in all weapons by 6 September and imposed a curfew from 6 p.m. to 7 a.m. On 8 September a German inspection at a house of the Brothers of the Christian Schools found two razors and parts of a Polish uniform. Two brothers, the father of one of them, three men from one family and two workers were arrested, taken to the barracks and later driven to a forest near the city and shot, according to the same article. On 10 September, it adds, the Germans carried out another large-scale roundup, which the article puts in quotation marks as a cleansing action, detaining hundreds of Polish and Jewish men, and sending 700 of them to civilian prisoner camps in the Reich.

The article also notes a detail about publicity. Western European media had reported on 2 September that the German air force had bombed the Jasna Góra monastery, which houses the Black Madonna icon. After the city was taken, on 5 September, the American journalist Louis P. Lochner was brought there at the invitation of Joseph Goebbels, and he confirmed that the monastery and icon had not been touched. According to Blisko Polski he did not know about the massacre that had happened the day before. The IPN's lecture notice mentions a further question for historians: what role Polish bomber pilots played in bringing the executions to an end.

Blisko Polski writes that after the war not one perpetrator was punished, and that a commemorative plaque was the response. It also draws on research by the historian Jochen Bochler (the spelling Blisko Polski prints), who it says found German documents that undercut the occupiers' claim that civilians and partisans provoked the shooting. Bochler's view, as relayed there, is that this and similar incidents arose because German recruits were inexperienced and unused to the conduct of war; the article adds that the German command knew this and ordered soldiers to empty their magazines before entering Częstochowa. After such events, the same article says, the German side adopted a standard account in which shootings were always blamed on Polish partisans and bandits.

The IPN has kept the event in public view. In February 2024 its Katowice branch held a lecture on Bloody Monday at its education centre in Częstochowa, given by the historian Adam Kurus; more than 100 people came to a room meant for about 50, and the IPN wrote that the event is still too little known and too rarely spoken of, even in Częstochowa itself. On 4 September 2020, the 81st anniversary, the 13 victims found in 2019 were buried in a common grave at the municipal cemetery on Radomska Street after a Mass in the cemetery chapel. Representatives of the IPN, the city and state authorities, soldiers from a commando unit and schools attended. In his speech, Adam Siwek, director of the IPN's Office of Commemoration of Struggle and Martyrdom, said that the catalogue of places where victims of war lie remains open. In 2026, the 87th anniversary, the IPN's Katowice branch again published a text by Kurus, which wPolsce24 reported.
